title: Google Associate Cloud Engineer
summary: The Google Associate Cloud Engineer credential, exam code ACE, is an entry to mid level certification from Google Cloud for people who deploy and operate workloads on that platform. It suits system administrators, cloud engineers and support staff with roughly six months of hands on Google Cloud experience. Passing it shows an employer that you can set up a cloud project, deploy an application, monitor its health and manage identity, networking and cost controls with the console and the command line. The exam is scenario based and uses multiple choice questions along with questions that have more than one correct answer. It leads to roles such as cloud engineer, cloud administrator, site reliability technician, DevOps engineer or cloud operations analyst. Google publishes the domain list, and the weightings below follow that published exam guide. Check the vendor current version before you book. This is an independent study guide and it is not approved or sponsored by Google.

beginner.definition: This is a certification from Google Cloud about running systems on Google Cloud. Google Cloud is a service that rents computers, storage and software over the internet. The exam checks that you can create a project, put an application online and keep it healthy. It is aimed at people who already use the platform a little.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many companies now run part of their work in a public cloud, so they need people who can operate it safely. This certificate proves you can do everyday cloud tasks without close supervision. It sits below the professional level exams, so it is a good first cloud goal. It shows an employer that you understand cost, identity and monitoring, not only how to click buttons. It also gives you a base for more advanced cloud roles later.
howItWorks: Start with the basics of cloud computing, including what a project, a region and a zone mean.
Learn the main building blocks, such as virtual machines, storage buckets, containers and managed databases.
Create your own free tier account so you can practise with real services instead of only reading.
Study the command line tool and the infrastructure as code option, because the exam asks about automation.
Work through each published domain in order and write short notes you can review again later.
Finish with practice questions that use scenarios, so you get used to choosing between two close answers.
beginner.example: Think of a small bakery that wants to sell cakes online. As the cloud engineer, you choose where the website lives, you give the staff accounts with the right permissions, and you set a budget alert so the bill never surprises the owner. When the site slows down on a busy morning, you look at the monitoring dashboards and find the cause. The exam gives you stories like this and asks which action you should take first. Most wrong answers are technically possible but careless, for example giving everyone the owner role or turning off logging to save money.
takeaways: You need hands on practice, because reading alone is not enough for scenario questions.
Learn identity and access management early, since it appears in several domains at once.
Watch your spending on your practice project, and set a budget alert from day one.

objectives: Explain how Google Cloud organises resources into projects, folders and an organisation.
Create and configure billing accounts, budgets and cost controls for a project.
Plan a deployment by choosing a region, a zone and an appropriate service type.
Deploy applications using virtual machines, containers and managed platforms.
Implement storage options and decide when object storage is the right choice.
Use monitoring, logging and alerting to keep an environment healthy.

chapters.title: Setting up a cloud solution environment
objectives: Create projects and organise them with folders so ownership is clear.
Link a billing account and set budgets and alerts for each project.
Install the command line tools and manage several configurations on one workstation.
Use infrastructure as code to create repeatable environments instead of hand made ones.
Grant roles to people and service accounts following the principle of least privilege.

chapters.title: Planning and configuring a cloud solution
objectives: Choose a compute option that matches the workload and the budget.
Plan network ranges, subnets and firewall rules before anything is deployed.
Select storage and database services based on how the data will be read and written.
Estimate the monthly cost of a design and explain the main cost drivers.
Decide where data must live to satisfy legal or latency requirements.

chapters.title: Deploying and implementing a cloud solution
objectives: Deploy virtual machine instances and adjust them when demand changes.
Run container images on a managed platform and expose them to users.
Load data into storage and database services and check that it arrived intact.
Publish an application so that users can reach it from the internet.
Apply the deployment through automation so the same result can be repeated.

chapters.title: Ensuring successful operation of a cloud solution
objectives: Read logs and metrics to find why a service is failing or slow.
Create alerts and dashboards that warn the team before users complain.
Manage the lifecycle of compute resources, including stopping idle machines.
Apply patches and configuration changes without taking the service down.
Use managed services and automation to reduce routine manual work.

chapters.title: Configuring access and security
objectives: Manage identity and access for users, groups and service accounts.
Audit access by reviewing role bindings and the audit log.
Protect data at rest and in transit with the available encryption options.
Harden a network with firewall rules, private addresses and secure entry points.
Investigate a security event using the logs the platform records.
